title: SHE DIED NAMING HIM AFTER HER PAIN. HIS FATHER REFUSED TO LET THAT BE HIS IDENTITY.
paragraphs: SHE DIED NAMING HIM AFTER HER PAIN. HIS FATHER REFUSED TO LET THAT BE HIS IDENTITY.

She called him the son of her sorrow. His father called him the son of his right hand. What happened on that road thousands of years ago may change the way you see your wounds, your identity, and the redeeming power of Jesus Christ.
Imagine carrying a child for months, dreaming about the life you would give him, only to realize that bringing him into this world would mean leaving it yourself.
No opportunity to watch him grow.
No opportunity to hear him call you Mother.
No opportunity to hold his hand through the difficult seasons of his life.
Just enough strength to give him a name before taking your final breath.
That is what makes one of the most heartbreaking moments in Genesis so difficult to read.
And perhaps what makes it even more personal is that some of us are still living under names given to us during somebody else's season of pain.
Names we never chose.
Identities we never deserved.
Labels that followed us long after the people who gave them to us were gone.
But what if your pain was never supposed to have the final authority over who you are?
Genesis 35:16–19 records the devastating final moments of Rachel, the beloved wife of Jacob.
They were traveling from Bethel toward Ephrath, later identified as Bethlehem, when Rachel went into extremely difficult labor.
This was the woman who had once cried out in desperation, “Give me children, or else I die” (Genesis 30:1, KJV).
Now, in a heartbreaking turn of events, she was dying while bringing her second son into the world.
The midwife attempted to comfort her.
“Fear not; thou shalt have this son also.” — Genesis 35:17 (KJV)
But Rachel would not survive.
And in the final moments of her life, Scripture records something extraordinary.
“And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Benoni: but his father called him Benjamin.” — Genesis 35:18 (KJV)
The original Hebrew reads:
וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ בֶּן־אוֹנִי וְאָבִיו קָרָא־לוֹ בִנְיָמִין
Vattiqra shemo Ben-Oni, ve'aviv qara-lo Vinyamin.
“She called his name Ben-Oni, but his father called him Benjamin.”
Ben-Oni (בֶּן־אוֹנִי) is traditionally understood in this context as “son of my sorrow” or “son of my suffering.”
Benjamin (בִּנְיָמִין) is traditionally understood as “son of the right hand.”
In biblical imagery, the right hand frequently represents strength, honor, authority, and favor (Psalm 110:1; Psalm 118:16).
The Hebrew word translated as “sorrow” has other possible nuances in different contexts, but Rachel's dying circumstances strongly support the traditional understanding of her son's name.
One child.
Two names.
One devastating moment.
Two profoundly different ways of identifying the life that would continue after it.
Rachel named him from within her suffering.
Jacob gave him another name.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us what Jacob was thinking when he changed the child's name. We should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But the contrast between those two names is undeniable.
And there is something deeply moving about it.
The circumstances surrounding Benjamin's birth were tragic, but tragedy did not remain his name.
Jacob could not reverse what had happened.
He could not bring Rachel back.
He could not erase the grief of that road.
Changing the child's name did not change the circumstances of his birth.
Rachel was still buried near Bethlehem. Jacob even erected a pillar over her grave, according to Genesis 35:20.
The sorrow was real.
The loss was permanent in this earthly life.
Yet the child would carry a different name.
Perhaps that is where this ancient story begins to collide with your own.
Maybe nobody literally named you Ben-Oni.
But life found other ways of calling you the child of sorrow.
The unwanted child.
The disappointing son.
The difficult daughter.
The abandoned spouse.
The failed parent.
The addict.
The adulterer.
The hypocrite.
The family embarrassment.
The Christian who fell again.
The person everyone remembers for the worst thing they ever did.
Perhaps someone wounded you so deeply that their words became the voice inside your head.
Perhaps your parents were carrying unresolved pain, and you grew up absorbing the consequences of wounds you did not create.
Perhaps you were born into poverty, rejection, broken relationships, or a household where love always seemed conditional.
Or perhaps the name you carry today came from something you actually did.
Something you cannot blame on your childhood.
Something you cannot excuse by pointing toward somebody else's behavior.
Something you would give almost anything to undo.
And now, whenever you try to pray, whenever you try to worship, whenever you try to believe that God could still use your life, a familiar accusation rises within you.
“Remember what you did.”
“Remember who you hurt.”
“Remember how many times you promised to change.”
“Remember what everybody knows about you.”
You may have spent years answering to a name that your heavenly Father never intended to define your entire existence.
But here is where we must understand the Gospel correctly.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve your self-esteem.
He did not come to tell you that your sins were insignificant, that your choices had no consequences, or that every uncomfortable accusation against you was false.
Some accusations may be true.
Some wounds were inflicted by you.
Some relationships were damaged because of your decisions.
Biblical grace does not require us to rewrite history dishonestly.
It calls us to bring the truth into the light.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that you were never guilty.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save the guilty.
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.” — Luke 19:10 (KJV)
The beauty of redemption is not that God pretends the scandal never happened.
The beauty of redemption is that the scandal does not have to become the final chapter of a life surrendered to Christ.
The apostle Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:17:
The original Greek contains the expression:
καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis
Meaning “new creation.”
Notice that Paul does not merely describe a new reputation, a new public image, or a more respectable version of your former self.
He speaks of new creation.
And the foundation of that transformation is found in two words:
In Christ.
Not in your ability to impress religious people.
Not in your perfect attendance at church.
Not in your ability to hide your struggles.
Not in the money you give.
Not in how successfully you convince the world that you have changed.
In Christ.
Through His death and resurrection, sinners who repent and believe receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
This is not positive thinking.
This is redemption.
This is why the same apostle who once persecuted the Church could later proclaim the Gospel he had previously attempted to destroy.
This is why Peter's denial of Jesus did not have to be the end of his discipleship.
This is why the thief on the cross could receive Christ's promise of paradise even when he had no remaining lifetime in which to rebuild his earthly reputation.
Grace did not make their pasts imaginary.
Grace demonstrated that Jesus was greater than their pasts.
And there is another remarkable detail in Rachel's story that deserves our attention.
She died on the way to Bethlehem.
Generations later, according to Matthew 2:1, Jesus Christ would be born in Bethlehem.

We must be careful here. Genesis does not explicitly present Benjamin's renaming as a direct prophecy about Jesus. But when we read these events within the wider biblical story, the geographical connection offers a deeply moving reflection.
Near Bethlehem, a mother died while bringing her son into the world.
In Bethlehem, centuries later, the Son of God entered the world, taking on human flesh, and would eventually give His life to redeem sinners.
The One born in Bethlehem would Himself become intimately acquainted with sorrow.
Isaiah 53:3 describes the suffering servant as:
“A man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
The Hebrew expression is:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת — ish makh'ovot
Literally, “a man of pains” or “a man of sorrows.”
The Christian understanding of Isaiah 53 finds its fulfillment in the suffering of Jesus Christ, as reflected in Acts 8:32–35 and 1 Peter 2:24.
Jesus did not remain distant from the suffering of humanity.
He entered it.
He experienced rejection.
He experienced betrayal.
He experienced grief.
He bore our sins upon the cross.
And after His resurrection, Scripture declares that He is seated at the right hand of God (Hebrews 1:3; Romans 8:34).
The One acquainted with sorrow is now exalted at the right hand of the Father.
And because of Him, those who belong to Christ are no longer defined solely by their former bondage to sin.
Romans 8:15 introduces another beautiful Greek word:
υἱοθεσία — huiothesia
Meaning “adoption” or “adoption as sons.”
It describes the believer's gracious reception into God's family through Christ.
You are not simply a criminal whose record has been forgiven.
Through Christ, you are welcomed into the family of God.
You are given a relationship you could never purchase, earn, or manufacture through religious performance.
And perhaps that is the truth somebody reading this desperately needs today.
You have been trying to earn a place at a table where Christ invites you through grace.
You have been punishing yourself for sins you have already sincerely confessed.
You have been confusing repentance with endless self-hatred.
But genuine repentance is not spending the rest of your life despising yourself.
It is turning away from sin and turning toward God.
It involves humility, confession, obedience, and a willingness to make restitution where possible.
It does not demand that you remain spiritually imprisoned forever.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1 (KJV)
That does not mean there will never be correction.
It does not mean consequences will disappear.
It does not mean healing will happen overnight.
It means that condemnation no longer has the final word over those who are in Christ.
There is a difference between the conviction that calls you out of darkness and the despair that tells you there is no reason to leave it.
Godly sorrow leads toward repentance, as Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 7:10.
The Gospel gives you a reason to get up, confess the truth, seek forgiveness, pursue holiness, and begin walking faithfully again.
Even when your voice shakes.
Even when people remember.
Even when rebuilding takes years.
Even when the consequences of yesterday are still waiting for you tomorrow morning.
Benjamin's new name did not erase Rachel's grave.
And your redemption may not erase every earthly consequence of your past.
But your past does not possess greater authority than Jesus Christ.
Please remember that.
Especially on the nights when you cannot sleep.
Especially when you see the people you disappointed.
Especially when an old memory returns and makes you feel unworthy of praying.
Especially when the enemy of your soul would rather have you hiding from God than running toward Him.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent of what needs to be abandoned.
Seek reconciliation where it is appropriate and possible.
Accept accountability.
And trust the Savior whose blood is sufficient to cleanse those who come to Him in faith.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
Perhaps you are not the person who caused the wound.
Perhaps you are the person who inherited it.
You are still grieving a mother, a father, a child, a marriage, or a childhood you never truly had.
Please do not read Rachel's story as though sorrow itself were something shameful.
Jesus wept.
The Psalms are filled with lament.
Grief is not necessarily evidence of unbelief.
You can love God deeply and still cry over what you have lost.
You can trust His promises and still need time to heal.
You can belong to Jesus and still have difficult days.
Christian hope does not demand that you pretend the grave is empty when someone you love has died.
Christian hope rests in the truth that Christ Himself rose from the grave, and that death will not have the ultimate victory over those who belong to Him.
Your tears are not an embarrassment to God.
And your suffering is not the entirety of your identity.
If these words have reached a place in your heart that you rarely allow anyone to see, perhaps today is the day to stop carrying everything in silence.
You do not owe the internet the private details of your wounds. Sometimes a simple request for prayer is enough.
And if you see someone else asking for prayer, take a moment to pray for them.
Let this become more than a comment section.
Let it become a place where wounded people are reminded of the truth, where repentance is encouraged, where grace is not cheapened, and where Jesus Christ receives the glory.
You may never know who reads it.
You may never see the tears behind their screen.
But you can make the truth of the Gospel available to someone who desperately needs to hear it.
That is one meaningful way to participate in the work of encouraging others toward Christ.
Our desire is not merely to fill your newsfeed with religious content.
It is to help bring biblical truth into the ordinary, painful, complicated realities of human life.
To reach the believer who is exhausted.
The Christian who has become spiritually complacent.
The seeker who has questions.
The person who has walked away from church.
And the sinner who wonders whether there is still a way home.
It also teaches that giving should come from a willing heart.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
It is not a mandatory tithe, a replacement for your responsibilities to your local church, or a payment for God's favor.
Salvation is freely given through the grace of Jesus Christ.
These benefits are our way of thanking those who choose to stand alongside this ministry.
But the greater purpose is helping the message of Scripture reach beyond the people who are already reading it.
If you believe this work is worth continuing, and you have the means and willingness to support it, we would be grateful to have you alongside us.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Now, before you leave, return for a moment to that road outside Bethlehem.
A mother was dying.
A father was grieving.
A newborn child entered a world he could not yet understand.
Rachel's final words gave him a name connected to her suffering.
But the name by which Scripture would remember him was Benjamin.
The sorrow remained part of his story.
It did not remain his name.
And while Genesis does not promise that every earthly tragedy will be reversed, the Gospel gives us something greater than the promise of an easier life.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Redeemer who brings forgiveness to the guilty.
The risen Lord who gives eternal hope to the grieving.
The One who can transform a life without pretending its darkest chapters never existed.
So stop believing that your worst chapter has already determined the ending.
Bring your sorrow to Jesus.
Bring your scandal to Jesus.
Bring the sin you are ashamed to confess, the grief you cannot explain, and the broken pieces you do not know how to put together.
He is not asking you to manufacture a spotless history before coming to Him.
He is calling you to repent, believe, and follow Him.
Your scars may remain.
Your memories may remain.
Your earthly circumstances may take time to change.
But in Christ, your standing before God is no longer determined by the darkest chapter of your former life.
The grave beside the road was real, but it was not the end of Benjamin's story. And the darkest chapter of your life does not have to be the final word over yours.
